summary: Sedating first-generation antihistamine with anti-nausea effects. Can knock down nausea and make you sleepy fast, but it’s high-risk in young kids and the injectable form can cause severe tissue injury.
description: Promethazine is a very sedating antihistamine that is sometimes used when nausea is fueling anxiety, insomnia or agitation, especially as a short-term rescue. The trade-off: it can cause heavy sedation, confusion, dry mouth, constipation and trouble peeing (anticholinergic side effects), and movement side effects (like muscle spasms). It has a boxed warning for fatal slowed breathing in children under 2. Promethazine injection can badly damage tissue and has caused tissue death (necrosis) and even amputations when given the wrong way.
patient_summary: Promethazine can calm nausea and make you sleepy pretty quickly — which is why some people feel “finally relaxed” after a dose. But it’s not a gentle sleep med. It can cause next-day grogginess, confusion, dry mouth/constipation, and (rarely) scary movement symptoms. It should NEVER be used in kids under 2. And the injectable version is notorious for severe tissue damage if it infiltrates or hits an artery.

primary.condition_name: Pain and sedation around childbirth (added to opioids)

off_label.context: Not a primary insomnia medication, but its strong sedation is sometimes leveraged short-term when nausea, vertigo, or acute illness is wrecking sleep. High side-effect burden limits routine use.
Not an anti-anxiety medicine, but when nausea is driving panic-like body symptoms, promethazine can calm things indirectly by easing nausea and causing sleepiness.
Sedation can reduce agitation in the short term, but promethazine can also cause delirium, akathisia, or paradoxical activation in some people — so it’s not a clean “calm-down” med.

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like being tranquilized. Expect impaired coordination and slowed thinking. If you need to be alert for work, school, driving, or childcare — treat that as a serious limitation.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble peeing, confusion (anticholinergic effects)
common_adverse_effects.notes: These effects are why it is often a poor fit for older adults. It can worsen constipation, trouble peeing and confusion, and the effects add up with other medicines that do the same.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: You can feel lightheaded or wobbly, especially after higher doses or parenteral administration. Falls are a real concern.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Movement side effects: strong inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms (dystonia), Parkinson-like stiffness, tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last)
common_adverse_effects.notes: These can look like restlessness, neck/jaw tightness, eye deviation, tremor, or stiffness. If you develop unusual muscle spasms or severe restlessness, get medical help — especially in kids and adolescents.

serious_risks.risk: Respiratory depression (rare but can be fatal, especially in children <2, excessive dosing, combined sedatives, or compromised respiratory function)
Severe tissue injury with injection (necrosis, thrombophlebitis, gangrene; may require surgical intervention including fasciotomy, grafting, or amputation)
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome): fever, rigid muscles, confusion, unstable heart rate or blood pressure. Get emergency help.
Severe delirium or deep confusion (higher risk when combined with other medicines that cause dry mouth, constipation and confusion, with overdose, or at older age)
Life-threatening arrhythmias related to altered cardiac conduction (reported with phenothiazines)

safety.black_box_warning: Promethazine must not be used in children younger than 2 because it can slow or stop breathing and cause death. Cases, including deaths, have been reported in this age group across a wide range of weight-based doses.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity or idiosyncratic reaction to promethazine, other phenothiazines, or any component of the formulation
Treatment of lower respiratory tract symptoms, including asthma
Children <2 years of age (boxed warning: risk of fatal respiratory depression)

precautions: Pediatrics ≥2 years: Use extreme caution, use the lowest effective dose, and avoid combining with other respiratory-depressant drugs
Breathing risk: avoid if you have weakened breathing or are at risk of breathing failure (for example COPD, sleep apnea)
CNS depression: Can cause marked drowsiness, delirium, impaired coordination, and slowed reaction time—higher risk with alcohol, opioids, and other sedatives
Severe tissue injury with injection: Promethazine injection has caused tissue necrosis, thrombophlebitis, gangrene, and amputations from inadvertent intra-arterial injection or extravasation

Injection limits: must never be injected into an artery or under the skin; IV use at concentrations above 1 mg/mL must not be used; deep injection into a muscle is the preferred route when an injection cannot be avoided
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome): reported with medicines that block dopamine, including promethazine; can be fatal
Cardiac conduction risk: Phenothiazines may alter conduction and have caused life-threatening arrhythmias

interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression: extreme sedation, impaired coordination, delirium risk, and potential respiratory compromise in vulnerable people.
Higher risk of profound sedation and respiratory depression, especially in people with sleep apnea, COPD, or other respiratory vulnerability.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking unless explicitly prescribed together with a clear plan and monitoring.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, cannabis)
interactions.mechanism: Sedation and cognitive impairment multiply. Fall risk and delirium risk increase — especially in older adults.
interactions.action: Use the lowest effective doses, avoid unnecessary combinations, and don’t assume “a little extra” is safe.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that cause dry mouth, constipation and confusion (anticholinergic medicines): many TCAs, some antipsychotics, benztropine, oxybutynin, diphenhydramine
interactions.mechanism: The effects add up: confusion, constipation, trouble peeing, blurred vision, delirium.
interactions.action: Keep the overlap as small as possible; think about the total load of these medicines, especially at age 65 and over.

interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of movement side effects and of a rare emergency with fever and rigid muscles (neuroleptic malignant syndrome).
interactions.action: Use cautiously and monitor for movement symptoms, fever/rigidity, and mental status changes.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Relief of symptoms (and whether sedation is helping or just impairing function)
Mental status and CNS effects: sedation, delirium, slowed reaction time, dizziness
Movement side effects: strong inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms (dystonia), shaking, Parkinson-like stiffness; watch closely in children
Breathing in people at high risk (sleep apnea, COPD, other medicines that slow the brain) and in children 2 and older if it is used
Dizziness when standing up and fall risk, especially in older adults

Signs and symptoms of tissue injury with parenteral administration: burning or pain at injection site, phlebitis, edema, skin discoloration; discontinue immediately if pain/burning occurs during IV infusion and evaluate for arterial injection or extravasation
Total load of medicines that cause dry mouth, constipation and confusion (anticholinergic medicines), especially at age 65 and over or when taking several of them

special_populations.pregnancy: There is outcome data from use in pregnancy. Promethazine crosses the placenta. It may be used as an add-on for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy when the preferred medicines do not help or symptoms continue. When taken within 2 weeks of delivery, it may affect how well the newborn's platelets help blood clot.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if promethazine is present in breast milk. Drowsiness and irritability have been reported in breastfed infants exposed to other antihistamines. Antihistamines may decrease maternal prolactin if given before lactation is established (effect observed after postpartum injection prior to breastfeeding). Manufacturer recommends deciding whether to discontinue breastfeeding or discontinue the drug, weighing importance to the mother. Single maternal doses may be compatible with breastfeeding; repeated doses should be avoided. Consider a second-generation antihistamine when an oral antihistamine is needed. Monitor infant for irritability, jitteriness, or drowsiness.
special_populations.pediatric: Should not be used in children under 2, because it can cause fatal slowed breathing (boxed warning). For children 2 and older: use extreme caution, the lowest dose that works, and avoid giving it with other medicines that slow breathing. Anti-nausea medicines are not recommended for simple vomiting in children; use is limited to long-lasting vomiting with a known cause. Avoid it in children who may have Reye syndrome or liver disease, because its side effects may be mistaken for signs of the illness.
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid use. Promethazine is listed as possibly inappropriate at age 65 and over because it strongly causes dry mouth, constipation and confusion (anticholinergic effects), with a higher risk of confusion and other effects of this kind. The body clears it more slowly with age, and people get used to it when it is used as a sleep medicine, which are further concerns. Taking other medicines with these effects at the same time raises the risk of falls, delirium and dementia, so the total load should be considered.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Adult: No dosage adjustment necessary for any degree of kidney dysfunction (only ~0.6% of dose excreted unchanged). Unlikely to be dialyzed; no supplemental dose needed. Pediatric: No dosage adjustments provided in manufacturer labeling.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Adults: the manufacturer gives no dose change; use with caution (a type of jaundice from blocked bile flow, cholestatic jaundice, has been reported). Children: the manufacturer recommends avoiding it in children with signs of liver disease, because its movement side effects may be confused with brain-related signs of liver disease.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid and complete after oral dosing, with significant first-pass effect
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral syrup: ~2.8 hours; Rectal: ~8.2 hours (adult data unless noted)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: IM: ~10 hours; IV: 9 to 16 hours; Suppositories/syrup: 16 to 19 hours (range: 4 to 34 hours)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic; hydroxylation via CYP2D6 and N-demethylation via CYP2B6; significant first-pass effect
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine and feces as inactive metabolites

dosing.titration: Promethazine is not dosed as a standard psychiatric medication. When it shows up in psychiatry-adjacent situations, it’s usually for short-term symptom relief where sedation is expected (and sometimes desired). Because of serious safety risks, especially in pediatrics and with injectable use, dosing should be conservative and individualized.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Promethazine does not typically require a taper when used short-term.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Promethazine is primarily an anti-nausea and motion-sickness medication — but in real life, people notice its strongest “psychiatric” effect: sedation. That sedation can be helpful short-term when nausea, vertigo, or acute illness is triggering anxiety, agitation, or insomnia. The downside is it’s not a targeted anxiety med — it’s a sedating, anticholinergic phenothiazine with real safety risks.
items: Short-term sedation when symptoms (like nausea/vertigo) are keeping you wired and unable to sleep
Nausea-driven anxiety: when your body symptoms are spiraling your mind, and you need a temporary off-switch
Adjunct sedation in monitored settings when used with other medications (with caution)
off_label: Insomnia (short-term, situational, generally avoided as a routine sleep med due to side effects)
Agitation (sedation may help, but risk of delirium/EPS makes it a non-ideal choice)
Anxiety (indirect benefit only; not a true anxiolytic)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: I took it and my brain just… powered down.
It didn’t fix my problems, but it made me stop caring for a few hours.
It’s not subtle. If you need to be functional, this might not be your friend.
items.note: Sedation can be intense and can linger into the next day.

quotes: Once the nausea eased up, my anxiety backed off too.
My panic was mostly my stomach. This helped the stomach, so the panic quieted.
items.note: Promethazine doesn’t treat anxiety directly — it can reduce the physical trigger and sedate you.

quotes: Dry mouth, blurry eyes, and constipation — like my whole system hit pause.
I felt foggy and kind of confused, especially standing up fast.
items.note: Anticholinergic effects can be rough: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion.

quotes: My neck felt tight and twisted — it freaked me out.
I felt restless in a way that didn’t match my mood, like I couldn’t sit still.
items.note: Extrapyramidal symptoms can happen (dystonia, akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia).

sections.intro: This med has a personality. For some people it’s “finally, sleep.” For others it’s “why do I feel like a dehydrated zombie?”

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Promethazine can hit quickly, especially by injection — but the “hangover” can last longer than people expect.
key_points: IV: ~5 minutes to start working (but IV use is high-risk and generally avoided)
Usually lasts 4 to 6 hours (can last up to 12 hours)
Sedation and slowed reaction time can show up within ~1 hour of ingestion and may persist after the “main” effect

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Promethazine isn’t a first-line psychiatric medication, and it’s not typically measured by anxiety or insomnia remission rates. Clinically, its usefulness in psychiatry is situational: strong sedation plus relief of nausea can temporarily reduce distress, improve sleep, and calm nausea-driven anxiety — but the side-effect burden and safety concerns limit how often it should be used.
sections.clinical_details: In psychiatry-adjacent use, the key question isn’t “Does it work?” — it’s “Is it worth the tradeoff today?” Sedation can be helpful in the short term, but the medication can cause delirium (especially in older adults), anticholinergic toxicity, extrapyramidal symptoms, orthostatic hypotension, and (in vulnerable patients) respiratory depression.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warning: Promethazine must NOT be used in children under 2 years due to risk of fatal respiratory depression.
sections.black_box: Promethazine must not be used in children younger than 2 because it can slow or stop breathing and cause death. Cases, including deaths, have been reported in this age group across a wide range of weight-based doses.
other: Pediatrics ≥2 years: Use extreme caution, use the lowest effective dose, and avoid combining with other respiratory-depressant drugs
Respiratory risk: avoid with compromised respiratory function or risk of respiratory failure (e.g., COPD, sleep apnea)
CNS depression: Can cause marked drowsiness, delirium, impaired coordination, and slowed reaction time—higher risk with alcohol, opioids, and other sedatives
Severe tissue injury with injection: Promethazine injection has caused tissue necrosis, thrombophlebitis, gangrene, and amputations from inadvertent intra-arterial injection or extravasation

Injection route restrictions: Contraindicated intra-arterial and subcutaneous; IV use at concentrations >1 mg/mL is contraindicated; deep IM is the preferred parenteral route when injection is unavoidable
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare): Reported with dopamine receptor antagonists, including promethazine; can be fatal
Cardiac conduction risk: Phenothiazines may alter conduction and have caused life-threatening arrhythmias
patient_counseling: If you’re using this for sleep or to calm symptoms, plan for sedation. Don’t drive, don’t drink alcohol, and don’t stack other sedatives unless your clinician explicitly tells you to.
If you have asthma, COPD, sleep apnea, or any breathing issues, this medication can be dangerous — bring that up before you take it.
Kids under 2: this is a hard no. For ages 2 and up, use the absolute lowest effective dose and avoid other meds that slow breathing.
Injection warning: If you ever receive injectable promethazine and it burns, hurts, or your skin changes color at the site, that’s an emergency-level signal. Tell staff immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are heavy sedation and anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision). In some people it can trigger delirium or movement symptoms (EPS). Rarely, it can contribute to respiratory depression in high-risk patients.
plain_language_list: Dizziness, slowed reaction time, motor instability
Confusion or delirium (higher risk in older adults)
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision (anticholinergic effects)
Extrapyramidal symptoms (restlessness, dystonia, tremor — uncommon but important)

common.patient_note: This can feel like being tranquilized. Expect impaired coordination and slowed thinking. If you need to be alert for work, school, driving, or childcare — treat that as a serious limitation.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion)
common.patient_note: The anticholinergic load is why this is often a bad fit for older adults. It can worsen constipation, urinary retention, and confusion — and it stacks with other anticholinergic meds.
You can feel lightheaded or wobbly, especially after higher doses or parenteral administration. Falls are a real concern.

common.symptom: Extrapyramidal symptoms (akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia)
common.patient_note: These can look like restlessness, neck/jaw tightness, eye deviation, tremor, or stiffness. If you develop unusual muscle spasms or severe restlessness, get medical help — especially in kids and adolescents.

serious: Respiratory depression (rare but can be fatal, especially in children <2, excessive dosing, combined sedatives, or compromised respiratory function)
Severe tissue injury with injection (necrosis, thrombophlebitis, gangrene; may require surgical intervention including fasciotomy, grafting, or amputation)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability) — medical emergency
Severe delirium or profound confusion (higher risk with anticholinergic burden, overdose, or older age)
Life-threatening arrhythmias related to altered cardiac conduction (reported with phenothiazines)

sections.intro: Promethazine is a sedation amplifier. The most dangerous combinations are the ones that also slow your brain and breathing.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Promethazine does not typically require a taper when used short-term.
key_points: Promethazine does not typically require a taper when used short-term.
If it’s being used repeatedly for sleep or sedation, discuss the pattern — because the bigger issue is usually side effects, falls, delirium risk, and medication stacking, not withdrawal.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Promethazine is not dosed as a standard psychiatric medication. When it shows up in psychiatry-adjacent situations, it’s usually for short-term symptom relief where sedation is expected (and sometimes desired). Because of serious safety risks, especially in pediatrics and with injectable use, dosing should be conservative and individualized.

adult.prn_sedation_context: Oral/rectal: 12.5 to 25 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed (short-term use is typical). Some experts recommend a maximum dose of 50 mg/day to avoid intolerable adverse effects.
adult.adjunct_opioids_sedation: IM (preferred) or IV (alternative): 25 mg once; may repeat every 4 hours for up to 2 additional doses (used as adjunct to opioids in peripartum management).
adult.parenteral_safety: IV and IM administration is generally avoided due to risk of severe tissue damage and chemical irritation. If IV is unavoidable: dilute to a concentration ≤1 mg/mL and infuse through a catheter in a large vein (not hand/wrist), preferably via a central venous catheter. Do not administer IV at concentrations >1 mg/mL. Do not administer intra-arterial or subcutaneous.

sections.simple_explanation: This medication is sedating by design. If you’re using it to help you settle or sleep, treat it like a heavy sedative: avoid alcohol, avoid stacking other downers, and assume you might be impaired for hours.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Promethazine has specific high-stakes cautions in pediatrics and older adults due to respiratory and anticholinergic risks. Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions should weigh symptom severity and safer alternatives.
sections.pregnancy: Outcome data following maternal use are available. Promethazine crosses the placenta. It may be used as adjunctive therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy when preferred agents don’t provide improvement or when symptoms persist. Platelet aggregation may be inhibited in newborns following maternal use within 2 weeks of delivery.
sections.lactation: It is not known if promethazine is present in breast milk. Drowsiness and irritability have been reported in breastfed infants exposed to other antihistamines. Antihistamines may decrease maternal prolactin if given before lactation is established (effect observed after postpartum injection prior to breastfeeding). Manufacturer recommends deciding whether to discontinue breastfeeding or discontinue the drug, weighing importance to the mother. Single maternal doses may be compatible with breastfeeding; repeated doses should be avoided. Consider a second-generation antihistamine when an oral antihistamine is needed. Monitor infant for irritability, jitteriness, or drowsiness.
sections.pediatrics: Contraindicated in children under 2 because of the potential for fatal respiratory depression (boxed warning). For children 2 and older: use extreme caution, use the lowest effective dose, and avoid giving it with other drugs that depress breathing. Antiemetics are not recommended for uncomplicated vomiting in children; limit use to prolonged vomiting of known cause. Avoid in children who may have Reye syndrome or liver disease, because side effects may be confused with the underlying illness.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid use. Promethazine is identified as potentially inappropriate in patients ≥65 due to potent anticholinergic properties and increased risk of confusion, dry mouth, constipation, and other anticholinergic toxicity. Reduced clearance with age and tolerance when used as a hypnotic are additional concerns. Exposure to concurrent anticholinergic drugs increases risk of falls, delirium, and dementia; consider total anticholinergic burden.
sections.hepatic: Adults: no manufacturer-provided dose adjustment; use with caution (cholestatic jaundice has been reported). Children: the manufacturer recommends avoiding use in children with signs and symptoms of liver disease (EPS may be confused with CNS signs of liver disease).
sections.renal: Adult: No dosage adjustment necessary for any degree of kidney dysfunction (only ~0.6% of dose excreted unchanged). Unlikely to be dialyzed; no supplemental dose needed. Pediatric: No dosage adjustments provided in manufacturer labeling.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Relief of symptoms (and whether sedation is helping or just impairing function)
Mental status and CNS effects: sedation, delirium, slowed reaction time, dizziness
Extrapyramidal symptoms: akathisia, dystonia, tremor, parkinsonism; watch closely in children
Respiratory status in people at high risk (sleep apnea, COPD, concurrent CNS depressants) and in children 2 and older if used
Orthostatic symptoms and fall risk, especially in older adults

Signs and symptoms of tissue injury with parenteral administration: burning or pain at injection site, phlebitis, edema, skin discoloration; discontinue immediately if pain/burning occurs during IV infusion and evaluate for arterial injection or extravasation
Total anticholinergic burden (especially in patients ≥65 or those on multiple anticholinergic medications)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Promethazine comes in oral, rectal, and injectable forms. The injectable version is high-risk for severe tissue injury, so many safety organizations discourage its use.
items: Oral solution: 6.25 mg/5 mL; 12.5 mg/10 mL
Injection solution: 25 mg/mL; 50 mg/mL (vesicant; significant tissue injury risk)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Promethazine is a phenothiazine derivative that blocks H1 histamine receptors (sedation), has anticholinergic (muscarinic-blocking) effects, and also blocks postsynaptic dopaminergic receptors in the brain. That mix explains both its “calm/sleepy” effect and its downside profile: confusion, dry mouth/constipation, and (in some people) movement symptoms.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, promethazine is not a first-line treatment for anxiety, insomnia, or agitation. Its role is situational: short-term, symptom-driven sedation when nausea/vertigo/acute illness is feeding distress and sleep loss. Because it’s strongly sedating and anticholinergic — and because pediatrics and injectable use carry serious safety warnings — it’s usually a last-mile option rather than a routine plan.

faqs.a: Not really. Promethazine is not a true anti-anxiety medicine. If it helps anxiety, it is usually indirect: it eases nausea and makes you sleepy, which can quiet anxiety driven by body symptoms. That is not the same as treating an anxiety disorder.

It can make you very sleepy, sometimes heavily so. But it is not a good insomnia medicine. The next-day fog, dry mouth, constipation and confusion it can cause (anticholinergic effects) are why many clinicians avoid it as a regular sleep plan, especially in older adults.
Onset can be quick: about 20 minutes after oral or IM dosing and about 5 minutes after IV dosing. Duration is usually 4 to 6 hours, but effects can last up to 12 hours.

faqs.q: Why is promethazine dangerous for young children?
faqs.a: There is a boxed warning: promethazine must not be used in children under 2 because of the risk of fatal respiratory depression. Postmarketing cases — including deaths — have occurred across a wide range of weight-based doses.

faqs.q: Is promethazine safe for kids over 2?
faqs.a: It can be used with extreme caution in children 2 and older, but the guidance is to use the lowest dose that works and avoid combining it with other medicines that slow breathing. Routine use has largely been replaced by other medicines with fewer side effects.

faqs.q: Can I take promethazine with alcohol?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus promethazine can cause heavy CNS depression: extreme sedation, impaired coordination, confusion, and higher risk of dangerous breathing suppression in vulnerable people.

faqs.q: Can promethazine cause delirium or confusion?
faqs.a: Yes. Promethazine can cause delirium, confusion, slowed reaction time and heavy sedation. The risk is higher in older adults and in people taking other sedating medicines or medicines that cause dry mouth, constipation and confusion (anticholinergic medicines).

faqs.q: What are movement side effects (EPS), and can promethazine cause them?
faqs.a: EPS are movement-related side effects like strong restlessness (akathisia), sudden muscle spasms (dystonia), stiffness or shaking (drug-induced parkinsonism), or tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last). Promethazine can cause EPS in both adults and children. If you get new muscle spasms, severe restlessness or abnormal movements, get medical care.

faqs.q: Why do people warn so much about promethazine injections?
faqs.a: Because severe tissue injury has been reported with promethazine injection, including tissue death (necrosis), gangrene, vein inflammation with clots (thrombophlebitis), and cases needing surgery to relieve pressure (fasciotomy), skin grafts or amputation. It must never be injected into an artery or under the skin. IV use has strict dilution and vein requirements and is generally avoided when safer options exist.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off promethazine?
faqs.a: Usually no. Promethazine doesn’t typically require a taper when used short-term. If you’re using it repeatedly for sleep or sedation, the bigger issue is safety and side effects — not withdrawal.

faqs.q: Is promethazine considered high-risk in older adults?
faqs.a: Yes. Promethazine is considered possibly inappropriate at age 65 and older because it strongly causes dry mouth, constipation and confusion (anticholinergic effects), with a higher risk of confusion, constipation, dry mouth, trouble peeing, delirium and falls, especially when combined with other medicines that have these effects.

seo.title: Promethazine (Phenergan): Sedation, Safety Warnings, Side Effects & Dosing Notes
seo.description: Promethazine (Phenergan/Promethegan) is a sedating antihistamine used for nausea and motion sickness that can also cause heavy sleepiness. Learn key risks: boxed warning in kids <2, respiratory depression risk, anticholinergic side effects, EPS, and severe tissue injury with injection.
